lessons.title: Identifying Opening and Closing Sentences
lessons.concept: In para jumbles, the opening sentence introduces the topic, context, or subject without depending on previous unexplained pronouns or references. The closing sentence often concludes, summarizes, or states a result/implication. Finding these anchors reduces possible arrangements.
lessons.formula: Opening cues: introduces a noun/topic, general statement, definition. Closing cues: therefore/finally/in conclusion/result, summary statement, consequence.
lessons.worked_example: Sentences: (A) Therefore, regular practice improves accuracy. (B) Aptitude tests measure problem-solving skills. (C) Many students prepare through timed exercises. (D) These skills include speed and logical thinking. A good flow: B (introduces topic) -> D -> C -> A (concludes).
mistakes: Choosing a sentence starting with a pronoun ('This/They/He') as opener without clear antecedent
Treating an example/detail as the opening instead of the topic statement
Ignoring concluding connectors like 'thus' or 'therefore' for the last sentence

lessons.title: Mandatory Pairs and Connectors
lessons.concept: Some sentences naturally follow each other: pronoun-noun links, cause-effect, problem-solution, general-specific, or sequence markers (first, then, finally). Transition words (however, moreover, for example, but, therefore) signal relationships that help pair sentences.
lessons.formula: Look for: noun -> pronoun reference, question -> answer, statement -> example, cause -> effect, contrast marker -> opposing idea.
lessons.worked_example: If one sentence mentions 'solar panels' and another begins with 'These devices', they likely form a pair. 'However' usually follows a contrasting statement, while 'For example' follows a general claim.
mistakes: Pairing sentences only by keyword overlap without checking logical flow
Ignoring contrast/addition connectors and creating broken logic
Missing pronoun references that require a prior noun

lessons.title: Building Coherent Sequence
lessons.concept: A coherent paragraph has a clear progression: introduction -> development/explanation/examples -> conclusion. After identifying anchors and pairs, test the full order by reading mentally: each sentence should connect to the previous one and move the idea forward.
lessons.formula: Check flow: topic introduced? terms defined before used? examples after claims? conclusion at end? no unexplained jumps.
lessons.worked_example: A paragraph on recycling: introduce recycling (what) -> explain process/benefits -> give example or impact -> conclude why it matters. Any order that gives an example before defining the topic is weak.
mistakes: Finalizing an order without reading the complete paragraph flow
Placing specific examples before the general statement they support
Breaking a mandatory pair to fit another guessed position

practice.question:
Arrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P: It converts sunlight into electricity.
Q: Solar energy is a renewable source of power.
R: This makes it useful for reducing dependence on fossil fuels.
S: A solar panel is a device used to capture this energy.
practice.explanation: Q introduces solar energy. S introduces the device that captures it ('this energy' refers to solar energy). P explains what it does. R concludes with its usefulness. Order: Q, S, P, R.

questions.question: A 'mandatory pair' in sentence rearrangement refers to:

options.A: Two sentences that can appear in any order
options.B: Two sentences that must be adjacent due to reference or connector links
options.D: Only the first and last sentences

questions.explanation: Mandatory pairs are sentences locked together by pronoun reference, connector words, or cause-effect links; breaking them apart breaks coherence.

questions.question: If sentence B contains the pronoun 'he', the sentence that introduces the person named should generally come:
questions.explanation: Pronouns follow their antecedents: the noun being referred to must appear before the pronoun, so the introducing sentence precedes B.
